extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners; corporate investor-relations and financial-communications specialists
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and managing financial/investor-relations communications and promotional/fund-raising campaigns, including objectives, target publics, communication channels, tactics, and program evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good communications (communication objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly half of respondents thought that if 'good communications exist ... other goals will fall into place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat clear, effective communication as foundational: measure whether target publics are being reached and informed (e.g., via surveys of analysts/shareholders). Good communication supports retention and acceptance objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a strong, ongoing relationship with analysts (symmetric communication objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and maintain long-term, two-way relationships with securities analysts so communication is not merely one-way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorized contacts, regular meetings, one-to-one visits, group seminars, presentations, plant tours, and timely responses to inquiries. Relationship-building is a primary long-term objective for financial PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop an informed market (message-retention objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an 'informed market' so investors can make intelligent, well-founded judgments about a company's prospects rather than rely on rumor or incomplete information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, interpretive financial information and simplify technical material (see financial-writing guidance). Use fact sheets, special publications, and explanatory materials to increase factual retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish credibility (message-acceptance / belief objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convince the investment community that information released is reliable by being honest in all relationships with investors and analysts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize honesty and transparency in disclosures and communications to build trust and acceptance of messages over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price / price-earnings (P/E) ratio as a behavior objective (with caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some companies measure success by the ratio of their stock price to profit level (P/E) as a long-term behavioral indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that P/E and stock price are influenced heavily by company performance and market forces; public relations alone cannot reliably increase P/E and thus should not be the principal evaluation metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: More than disclosure: interpret and simplify financial information
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial PR should go beyond 'disgorgement' of raw information to interpreting and simplifying data—especially for nonprofessional, small investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid releasing raw numbers without context. Provide explanations, interpretive commentary, and simplified presentation (see chapter on financial writing) so nonprofessional publics can retain and accept the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and segment financial publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial publics typically fall into four groups: current shareholders; prospective shareholders; the financial community (bankers, brokers, analysts, mutual fund/insurance/pension managers); and financial media (Wall Street Journal, Barron's, financial sections, specialized broadcast programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and tailor messages and channels for each group (e.g., analyst briefings vs. consumer-targeted notices). Accurate audience identification guides tactics and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess publics' situational characteristics to determine strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial publics are usually high in involvement and problem recognition and often low in constraint recognition—making them active publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use situational theory of publics to choose appropriate communication modes: active publics require detailed information and two-way interactions (e.g., analysts), whereas routine publics may need simpler reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel top management and analyze market trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial relations specialists should keep top management informed about stock-market status and explain reasons for significant changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely analyses and recommendations (e.g., reports on buying/selling trends, interpretations of causes) so management can adopt coherent financial-communications programs aligned with business principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate shareholder-communication materials and events
rubrics_metrics.description: Shareholder communications include printed materials (newsletters, magazines, quarterly reports, annual reports, company biographies, booklets), the annual meeting, proxy solicitations, and surveys of shareholder opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the annual report as the cornerstone of shareholder relations. Use varied printed and event-based tools to reach shareholders; ensure materials support communication, retention, and acceptance objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple channels for communication with professional analysts
rubrics_metrics.description: Common analyst contacts include telephone follow-ups, visits by individual analysts, group meetings/seminars, presentations at analysts' societies, travel to meet analysts, plant tours/field trips, special presentations at annual meetings, fact sheets/fact books, and dissemination of financial news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize one-to-one and small-group interactions for analysts, supplement with high-quality printed/reference materials, and ensure rapid, accurate responses to inquiries to build relationship and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate programs with analyst surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies conduct analyst surveys (in-house or via research firms) to determine whether analysts are satisfied and to rate handling of inquiries and usefulness of analyst-targeted publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include items that measure communication (exposure/handling), message acceptance (opinions about earnings/management/marketing), and message retention (factual questions). Use quantitative items where possible to track change over time (see Chapter 9 for sample questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analyst feedback and analysis of analysts' reports as qualitative measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial PR specialists use informal feedback, formal interviews, or by reading reports analysts write about the company to assess message-retention and message-acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative methods work well if observers explicitly look for indicators tied to communication, retention, and acceptance objectives. Triangulate qualitative findings with survey data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use behavioral measures and awards cautiously in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some specialists look at stock P/E ratios or institutional purchases as behavioral measures; others track awards from analyst or communications societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral measures (stock price, institutional buying) are useful but are strongly affected by company performance and should never be the principal evaluation criterion. Awards are nice but rarely measure specific communication objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate shareholder communication by measuring exposure, retention, and acceptance with representative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys of shareholders often measure overall attitudes; for communication objectives, questions should measure exposure to shareholder media, memory of information, and belief in the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mail questionnaires, telephone surveys, or representative sampling methods rather than relying solely on shareholder-meeting attendees (not a representative sample). Design questions to map to the three objectives (communication, retention, acceptance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select an appropriate communication model for promotion and fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion/fund-raising programs are often run according to the press agentry model or the two-way asymmetric model; the two-way symmetric model is more sophisticated and encourages mutual benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the two-way symmetric model when possible to promote exchange relationships and long-term behavior change; avoid purely one-way 'hype' approaches if the goal is sustained engagement or reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design promotion and fund-raising campaigns to provide reciprocal benefits and address barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Donors and audiences give time/money/attention only if they receive satisfaction, recognition, tax benefit, or other exchange value; behavior-change campaigns must address perceived costs/inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate donors (involve them in planning, offer recognition), and for public-communication campaigns (e.g., seat belts) identify and reduce barriers (e.g., convenience) or solicit public input on solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use targeted media-relations and supportive tactics for product publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective product publicity combines press kits, consumer hotlines, distribution of photos/articles, targeted audience angles, dealer relations, and promotional characters or events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor publicity tactics to audience segments (trade press vs consumer media), provide practical support (hotlines, installation guides), cultivate intermediaries (dealers), and use attention-getting but relevant angles to increase media pickup and retention (Genie case examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research, consumer services, and multimedia channels to support symmetric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that ask consumers what information they need and then simplify/present it (e.g., business-leadership programs, answer centers, toll-free numbers, multimedia presentations) exemplify symmetric communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate consumer research into program design; provide accessible service channels (databases, toll-free lines) and multimedia outreach to meet information needs and increase retention and acceptance.
